You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 69
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Nanny
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 71

# A Grandfather's Vigil

Marcus sits in the waiting room with his hands folded in his lap, his posture rigid despite the comfortable chair. At sixty-nine, he has the weathered appearance of someone who has spent decades in physical work, though his current job as a nanny for his two young grandchildren is what occupies most of his waking hours. He speaks softly, with the careful enunciation of someone for whom English is a second language, though he has lived in this country for forty years.

Four years ago, his youngest grandchild, Sophia, was five years old. Marcus had picked her up from kindergarten on a Tuesday afternoon as he did most days. She complained of a headache during the car ride home, something he thought nothing of—children were always catching small illnesses. By evening, she was burning with fever. Her mother, Marcus's daughter, was working late. He gave her acetaminophen and put her to bed, checking on her every thirty minutes as any careful grandfather would.

At two in the morning, Sophia seized. Marcus woke to her small body convulsing, her eyes rolled back. The terror that flooded through him was unlike anything he had ever experienced. He called 911 with shaking hands, performed CPR as the dispatcher instructed, and rode in the ambulance holding her limp hand. The hospital diagnosed bacterial meningitis. For three days, she hovered between life and death in the pediatric intensive care unit. Marcus barely left her bedside.

Sophia survived. She recovered fully, with no lasting neurological damage. By all measures, it was a miracle. Yet something inside Marcus fractured that night and has never fully mended.

Now, four years later, Marcus still wakes most nights at two o'clock. He doesn't know why his body has chosen that hour, but he jolts awake with his heart racing, drenched in sweat, reaching for a phone that isn't there. The first thing he does is check on his grandchildren, even though they are now safe in their beds. This ritual happens almost every night. Some mornings, he hasn't slept at all.

During the day, when he is caring for Sophia and her older brother, Marcus finds himself in a state of constant vigilance. He takes their temperatures obsessively—sometimes three or four times a day—even when they show no signs of illness. A small cough sends him into a spiral of "what ifs." He keeps a notebook where he tracks their symptoms, their eating habits, their energy levels. His daughter has gently suggested this is excessive, but he cannot stop. The fear that something catastrophic will happen again lives just beneath his skin.

Loud noises startle him profoundly. A car backfiring on the street, a child crying in a store, even his phone ringing—all send jolts of adrenaline through his body. He finds himself avoiding situations where he might encounter sick children or hospitals. He no longer volunteers at the community center as he once did. Television shows depicting medical emergencies are unwatchable; he leaves the room.

What troubles Marcus most is the guilt. Sophia was fine in the end. He knows this intellectually. Yet he replays that night endlessly, wondering if he should have recognized the symptoms sooner, called the ambulance faster, done something differently. He sometimes finds himself sitting alone in his small apartment, staring at nothing, consumed by the weight of what almost was.

His daughter worries about him. She sees how tired he looks, how his hands sometimes tremble when he is not actively caring for the children. She suggested he talk to someone, and after months of resistance, he finally agreed.
